subsections.subsection_title: What the OSCE station may say

blocks.text: You may encounter any of these scenarios:
Focused history: A 42-year-old woman presents with heavy menstrual bleeding and progressively worsening period pain. Take a focused history and outline your differential diagnoses.
Clinical examination: Examine a woman with suspected adenomyosis and report your findings.
Investigation interpretation: Interpret a pelvic ultrasound report showing a bulky, heterogeneous uterus with myometrial cysts.
Management counselling: Explain the diagnosis and treatment options to a woman with adenomyosis who has completed her family.
Differential diagnosis: Differentiate adenomyosis from uterine fibroids and endometriosis.
Fertility counselling: Discuss adenomyosis in a woman who wishes to become pregnant.

Adenomyosis is a benign uterine condition in which endometrial glands and stroma are present within the myometrium, the muscular wall of the uterus, usually with surrounding hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the muscle.
It can cause:
Heavy menstrual bleeding.
Severe dysmenorrhoea.
Chronic pelvic pain.
Deep dyspareunia.
An enlarged, tender uterus.
Reduced quality of life and, in some patients, fertility difficulties.
Adenomyosis is not cancer, although it can coexist with other uterine conditions.
Endometrial tissue is distributed throughout multiple areas of the myometrium. The uterus may be uniformly enlarged and bulky.
Disease is concentrated in a particular area of the uterine muscle, producing a localized lesion that may resemble a fibroid.
A less common pattern involving cystic spaces within the myometrium, sometimes containing blood products.
Start by saying:

“Good morning. My name is … I am a medical student/doctor. I understand you have been experiencing problems with your menstrual periods. I would like to ask you some questions about your symptoms, menstrual history, reproductive health and general wellbeing to help identify the possible cause. Some questions may be personal, but they are important for your care. Is that alright?”
Confirm the patient's identity, ensure privacy, obtain consent and offer a chaperone where appropriate.
Ask:
What brought you to the hospital today?
What is the main problem: heavy bleeding, painful periods, pelvic pain or something else?
When did the symptoms begin?
Have they been getting worse?
Do the symptoms affect your daily activities or work?
This is particularly important because adenomyosis commonly presents with heavy, painful periods.
Ask about:
Age at menarche.
Date of the last menstrual period.
Cycle regularity and length.
Duration of bleeding.
Amount of bleeding.
Passage of clots.
Flooding or bleeding through clothing.
Number of sanitary pads used and how often they are changed.
Night-time changes or double protection.
Intermenstrual bleeding.
Postcoital bleeding.
Dysmenorrhoea and whether it is progressive.
Important questions for heavy menstrual bleeding:
“Do you need to change your pad every hour or two?”
“Have you ever felt dizzy, faint or unusually tired during your period?”
“Has the bleeding prevented you from going to work or performing normal activities?”
These questions help assess severity and possible anaemia.
Use the SOCRATES framework.

rows: Is the pain in the lower abdomen, pelvis or back?
When did it start? Was it gradual or sudden?
Is it cramping, aching, sharp or pressure-like?
Does it spread to the back or thighs?
Is it associated with bleeding, dyspareunia or bowel symptoms?
Is it cyclical, occurring mainly during menstruation?
Does it worsen during periods? What relieves it?
How severe is it on a scale of 0–10?

blocks.text: Ask whether the pain is becoming progressively worse over months or years. Progressive dysmenorrhoea is a useful clue but is not specific to adenomyosis.
Ask about:
Chronic pelvic pain.
Deep pain during sexual intercourse.
Pressure or heaviness in the pelvis.
Urinary frequency or urgency.
Constipation or painful defecation, especially if cyclical.
Fatigue, breathlessness, palpitations or dizziness, suggesting anaemia.
Fever or offensive vaginal discharge, which may indicate another diagnosis.
Ask about:
Gravidity and parity.
Previous pregnancies, miscarriages and deliveries.
Caesarean section or other uterine surgery.
Previous diagnosis of fibroids or endometriosis.
Previous pelvic ultrasound or MRI.
Previous treatments and their effectiveness.
Contraception and hormonal medication.
Cervical screening history, as appropriate.
Adenomyosis is frequently diagnosed in women in their 30s and 40s and is more often recognized in those with previous pregnancies. However, it can occur in younger and nulliparous women too.
Ask:
Are you currently trying to conceive?
Have you had difficulty becoming pregnant?
Have you completed your family?
Would you consider hormonal treatment?
How important is preserving your uterus?
These questions directly affect management. For example, hysterectomy is definitive treatment but eliminates the possibility of carrying a future pregnancy.

content_groups.group_title: H. Relevant medical and family history

blocks.text: Ask about:
Bleeding disorders.
Thyroid disease.
Use of anticoagulants.
Personal or family history of gynaecological malignancy.
Other medical conditions that may affect treatment choice.
Explain the examination, obtain consent and offer a chaperone. Abdominal and pelvic examinations should be performed only when indicated, with appropriate privacy and respect.
Look for:
Pallor, suggesting anaemia.
Tachycardia or postural symptoms if bleeding has been substantial.
General distress due to pain.
Other signs suggesting an alternative diagnosis.
Example report:
“The patient is alert and comfortable at rest. There is mild conjunctival pallor, with no obvious respiratory distress. Her vital signs are …”
If the patient is unstable or actively bleeding heavily, assess and manage this urgently before proceeding with a routine examination.
Inspect for distension, scars and visible masses.
Palpate for:
A palpable suprapubic or pelvic mass.
Lower abdominal tenderness.
Uterine enlargement, if appreciable abdominally.
Guarding or rebound tenderness, which should prompt consideration of an acute abdominal or pelvic condition.
Adenomyosis may not produce a palpable abdominal mass, especially when the uterus is only mildly enlarged.
With informed consent and a chaperone, perform a speculum examination when indicated to assess the cervix and vaginal bleeding, followed by bimanual examination if appropriate.
Possible bimanual findings include:
A bulky, enlarged uterus.
A globular or rounded uterine contour.
A soft or boggy uterine feel.
Uterine tenderness.
Usually a relatively uniform enlargement in diffuse disease.
Possible coexisting adnexal or uterine pathology.
These findings are suggestive rather than diagnostic.

content_groups.group_title: D. Examples of abnormal examination reporting

blocks.text: “On bimanual examination, the uterus is mildly enlarged, globular and tender, with no palpable adnexal mass. These findings are suggestive of adenomyosis, although pelvic imaging is required for further assessment.”

“The patient appears mildly pale. Abdominal examination reveals mild suprapubic tenderness without guarding. Pelvic examination demonstrates a bulky, tender uterus. Given the history of heavy menstrual bleeding, I would assess for anaemia and arrange pelvic imaging.”

“The uterus is enlarged and irregular in contour. This is more suggestive of uterine fibroids, although adenomyosis may coexist. I would request pelvic ultrasound to characterize the uterine pathology.”

“The abdominal examination is unremarkable, and the uterus is not appreciably enlarged or tender on bimanual examination. Adenomyosis cannot be excluded on examination alone, so further assessment would depend on the clinical history and imaging findings.”

rows: Heavy, painful periods; bulky, tender, globular uterus
Heavy bleeding, pressure symptoms, irregularly enlarged uterus
Dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, cyclical bowel/bladder symptoms, possible infertility
Intermenstrual bleeding or heavy bleeding; focal lesion on imaging
Abnormal bleeding, particularly postmenopausal bleeding or bleeding with risk factors
Pelvic pain, discharge, fever or cervical motion tenderness
Irregular or unpredictable bleeding, often without a characteristic bulky tender uterus

blocks.text: Exam pearl: Adenomyosis and endometriosis can coexist. Heavy, painful periods and a globular, tender uterus suggest adenomyosis, while deep dyspareunia and cyclical bowel symptoms may raise suspicion for endometriosis.
Perform a urine or serum β-hCG test when pregnancy is possible. Pregnancy-related causes of pelvic pain or bleeding must be excluded.
Assess for anaemia in women with heavy menstrual bleeding.
Possible findings include:
Reduced haemoglobin.
Microcytosis and hypochromia if iron deficiency is established.
Other abnormalities suggesting alternative causes.
Ferritin may be useful when iron deficiency is suspected, depending on the clinical context.

Transvaginal ultrasound is generally the preferred first-line imaging test when appropriate and acceptable to the patient. Transabdominal ultrasound may be used when transvaginal imaging is unsuitable or declined.
Features that may suggest adenomyosis include:
Globular uterine enlargement.
Asymmetrical thickening of the myometrium.
Heterogeneous myometrial echotexture.
Small myometrial cysts.
Fan-shaped shadowing.
Echogenic subendometrial lines or buds.
An irregular or interrupted junctional zone.
No single ultrasound finding is sufficient in every case. Interpretation depends on the combination of features and the expertise of the person performing the scan.
MRI may be useful when ultrasound findings are inconclusive, when detailed mapping is required or when distinguishing adenomyosis from fibroids would change management.
Possible findings include:
Thickening of the junctional zone.
Low-signal-intensity areas within the myometrium on T2-weighted images.
Small high-signal foci representing ectopic endometrial tissue or associated cystic changes.
MRI is not necessary for every patient.
Endometrial biopsy does not diagnose adenomyosis because the condition is located in the myometrium.

However, endometrial sampling may be indicated to investigate other causes of abnormal uterine bleeding, depending on age, risk factors, persistence of symptoms and local guidelines. It is particularly important to evaluate postmenopausal bleeding.
Neither is routinely required to diagnose adenomyosis.
Hysteroscopy evaluates the uterine cavity and may help identify polyps or other intracavitary pathology.
Laparoscopy is more relevant when endometriosis or another surgically assessed pelvic condition is suspected.
Management depends on symptom severity, contraindications, reproductive plans and patient preference.
Assess the severity of bleeding and pain.
Check for anaemia and treat iron deficiency when present.
Exclude pregnancy and other relevant causes.
Review imaging and identify coexisting conditions.
Discuss whether the patient wishes to preserve fertility or the uterus.
Severe active bleeding with haemodynamic compromise requires urgent stabilization and specialist management.

Examples include ibuprofen or naproxen when appropriate. These can reduce menstrual pain and may reduce menstrual blood loss. Check contraindications, including renal disease, peptic ulcer disease and relevant medication interactions.

Often a useful option for heavy bleeding and dysmenorrhoea when the uterine cavity is suitable and there are no contraindications. Initial irregular bleeding may occur, and the patient should understand what to expect.
Combined pills, patches or rings may help regulate bleeding and reduce pain. Assess eligibility, including thromboembolic risk, migraine with aura, blood pressure and smoking-related risk.
Oral or other appropriate progestogen regimens can help control symptoms. Selection depends on the individual clinical circumstances and treatment goals.

These may be considered under specialist supervision for selected patients, particularly when other treatments are unsuitable or ineffective. Hypoestrogenic effects, bone health and the need for add-back therapy must be considered.

Tranexamic acid may also be considered for heavy menstrual bleeding when appropriate. It reduces bleeding but does not directly treat the underlying adenomyosis, and thrombotic history and other contraindications should be reviewed.

Hysterectomy: definitive treatment for adenomyosis in someone who does not wish to carry a future pregnancy. Discuss surgical risks, recovery, alternatives and the implications of removing the uterus.

Adenomyomectomy: may be considered in selected patients with focal disease, particularly when uterine preservation is important. It requires specialist assessment and carries risks, including uterine scarring and future pregnancy complications.
Uterine artery embolization: may be considered in selected patients, but suitability, effectiveness and fertility implications require specialist counselling.
Endometrial ablation: may improve bleeding in selected patients but does not reliably treat disease within the myometrium. It is unsuitable for those wishing to become pregnant in the future.
For a patient wishing to conceive:
Review age, duration of infertility and other fertility factors.
Consider referral to a fertility specialist.
Explain that the evidence linking adenomyosis to reduced fertility and pregnancy complications varies by patient and disease characteristics.
Discuss treatment options individually; hormonal suppression usually prevents conception while being used.
Explain that uterine surgery may create scarring and can affect future pregnancy management.
A good OSCE response might be:

“Your symptoms and examination findings raise the possibility of adenomyosis, a benign condition in which tissue similar to the lining of the womb is found within its muscular wall. It can make the womb enlarged and tender and can cause painful, heavy periods.
“We would usually arrange a pelvic ultrasound to assess the womb and look for other possible causes, such as fibroids. We would also check your blood count if you have been bleeding heavily.

“Treatment depends on how much the symptoms affect you and whether you wish to become pregnant in the future. Options include anti-inflammatory painkillers, hormonal treatments and a hormonal intrauterine system. If symptoms remain severe, a specialist can discuss procedural or surgical options. Hysterectomy is definitive, but it means you would no longer be able to carry a pregnancy.
“We can discuss the advantages, disadvantages and risks of each option and choose a plan that suits your needs.”
Invite questions and confirm the patient's understanding.

subsections.subsection_title: Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is adenomyosis?
Endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, usually associated with hypertrophy and hyperplasia of surrounding smooth muscle.
Q2. What are the classical symptoms?
Heavy menstrual bleeding, dysmenorrhoea and chronic pelvic pain. Some patients are asymptomatic.
Q3. What is the classical examination finding?
A bulky, globular, often tender uterus, although examination may be normal.
Q4. What is the first-line imaging investigation?
Transvaginal ultrasound when appropriate and acceptable.
Q5. What ultrasound features suggest adenomyosis?
A globular uterus, asymmetrical myometrial thickening, heterogeneous myometrium, myometrial cysts and fan-shaped shadowing, among other features.
Q6. How does adenomyosis differ from fibroids?

Fibroids are discrete benign smooth-muscle tumours that may distort the uterine contour. Adenomyosis involves endometrial tissue within the myometrium and more typically produces a globular, heterogeneous uterus. Both can coexist.
Q7. Is hysterectomy the only treatment?
No. Medical options include NSAIDs, tranexamic acid for bleeding, hormonal contraception, progestogens and the LNG-IUS. Hysterectomy is definitive but is not required for everyone.
Q8. Does endometrial biopsy diagnose adenomyosis?
No. The disease is within the myometrium. Biopsy may nevertheless be indicated to investigate endometrial pathology causing abnormal bleeding.
Q9. Can adenomyosis occur in a woman who has never been pregnant?
Yes. It is more commonly recognized in women in their 30s and 40s and those with previous pregnancies, but it can occur in nulliparous women and younger patients.
Q10. Can adenomyosis cause infertility?

It may be associated with reduced fertility in some patients, but the relationship varies. Fertility counselling should consider age, other fertility factors and the patient's individual circumstances.
Assuming that every woman with heavy, painful periods has adenomyosis.
Failing to consider fibroids, endometriosis and pregnancy-related causes.
Treating a normal ultrasound as proof that adenomyosis is absent.
Claiming that endometrial biopsy confirms adenomyosis.
Recommending hysterectomy without asking about future pregnancy plans.
Forgetting to assess for anaemia in heavy menstrual bleeding.
Failing to discuss treatment adverse effects and patient preference.

items: N — Normal or nonspecific examination can still occur
A — Assess anaemia and alternative diagnoses
C — Control bleeding with suitable medical treatment
T — Tailor treatment to fertility plans and symptom severity

blocks.text: 1. A 41-year-old woman has heavy painful periods and a bulky, tender, globular uterus. Which diagnosis is most suggestive?
2. Which is generally the first-line imaging investigation when appropriate?
3. Why does an endometrial biopsy not establish the diagnosis of adenomyosis?
Adenomyosis affects the myometrium rather than being confined to the endometrium
4. Which option is definitive for adenomyosis in a patient who does not desire future pregnancy?
5. A patient with suspected adenomyosis wants to conceive. What is the best general approach?

items: Use hormonal suppression while telling her it promotes conception
Individualize fertility assessment and refer for specialist advice when indicated
